In order to dispel the preceding obstacles and hope that you may suddenly forget all feelings of alarm and fear, so that everyone may abide in peace and composure,
I shall now reverently recite the Tathāgata’s Mantra for Dispelling Fear.
Oṃ tadyathā vadati dhane dhara-kī kuru durlabhe svāhā. (Having finished reciting the mantra three times, strike the cymbals.
[The Dharma Master visualizes:

Within the three miserable realms, there are countless sentient beings who, although they have reached this Dharma assembly, are obstructed by their evil karma and feel fear and trepidation in their hearts; now, by the power of this mantra, they immediately attain peace of body and mind.
"Peaceful! There is nothing like the fear of dread. (The ritual master rings the bell to open the throat and declares:
"That which is hideous in form is called a ghost; its head towers like a mountain peak, and its throat is as narrow as the eye of a needle."
Regretting that water and grain could not pass through, one truly realizes that hunger and deprivation are extreme. Although the three realms differ, the various classes of beings are numerous;
because their causal actions may be identical, their retributive fruits are similar. Thus, by proclaiming the secret [teachings], great parsimony and greed are utterly destroyed.
I hope that the food and drink will be sweet and harmonious, and that the throat and gullet will surely be relaxed and unobstructed.
The Buddha, the Tathāgata, possesses a mantra for opening the throat; I shall now reverently recite it.
Oṃ kili kumāri hūḷa hūḷa chala chala svāhā. (Having finished reciting the mantra three times, strike the cymbals.

(The Dharma Master visualizes the countless sentient beings within the three miserable realms who, due to their past karma, have constricted throats through which food and drink cannot pass; now, by the power of the mantra, they immediately attain expansion and breadth.)

(To remove all obstructions. (The ritual master rings the bell while reciting the *biaobai* [declaration]: "For the sake of the sentient beings of the six realms, I shall unravel their knots of resentment.
He declares: All phenomena are fundamentally empty; how could there be the marks of self or person? This mind is without faction; how can it harbor feelings of enmity or gratitude?"

Because they do not understand that external objects are not other, they falsely identify this body as "self. Thereupon, they address one another as "you" and "I," each establishing their own boundaries.
Due to even slight disagreements in intention or a lack of compliance in speech, they suddenly change countenance with resentment and hastily commit irrational acts of anger;
they abruptly give rise to hatred and consequently initiate groundless slanders. Those who possess [such tendencies]...
Relying on their status as elders, they deceive the orphaned and the widowed; dwelling in wealth and nobility, they oppress the lowly and the humble.

They encroach upon the lands of neighboring elders to expand their new dwellings, and seize the wealth of market-goers to fill their private treasuries. They recklessly inflict the cruelty of whips and canes, and unjustly impose the grievances of litigation and imprisonment.

Relying on power to overstep over others, they act with deceitful hearts and turn their backs on righteousness, greedily consuming flesh and blood to satisfy their own appetites. They are devoid of...
To harbor thoughts of harming life and to incite curses to provoke the spirits—how could such acts escape karmic retribution?
Thus, they take turns inflicting vengeance upon one another without end. All this stems from a single morning’s transgression, yet it causes calamity to persist through many kalpas.
Now, as the Three Honored Ones gather and beings from the six realms arrive, we shall together receive the true practice; first, however, we must dispel our long-standing grudges.

Once the heart of forbearance is aroused, how can the conditions of humiliation remain? Reflecting that enemies are originally one's own kin, and viewing both men and women as my own parents, may we forever dissolve our resentment and each give rise to profound joy.
With sleeves joined and skirts linked, let us proceed directly upon the path to Bodhi.

Their minds opened and their intentions were liberated; all ascended to the field of deliverance. As for your mother, she has lost this auspicious opportunity; you should now press forward to seek supreme benefit.
Our Buddha, the Tathāgata, possesses a mantra for resolving the knots of enmity; I shall now reverently recite it.
Oṃ santara khada svāhā. (Recite this mantra three times. It is even more excellent if the assembly recites it together many times.

The Dharma Master visualizes the sentient beings of the six realms who, since beginningless time, have constantly accumulated knots of resentment; now, upon hearing this dharani method, they all give rise to joyful hearts, and their animosities are simultaneously dissolved as they turn toward one another with mutual affection. (The ritual master rings the bell and makes the invocation for them to proceed to the bathhouse.)
He spoke, saying:
"The abodes of the six realms of existence are diverse, yet none are free from turbidity and evil. The retributions of the three miserable paths are most loathsome; they are entirely foul and putrid.

If one speaks merely in terms of external phenomena, one cannot avoid encountering obstacles within the mind. One must personally undergo purification through bathing, hoping thereby to attain [liberation]."

The refreshing water of the Dharma has just moistened you; behold the purity and brilliance of your entire body. A single breeze of compassion sweeps over you, causing your present mindfulness to open and become clear.
Do not linger out of habit; you should hasten forward with diligence.
(The assembly receives the Pure Way [the image] and escorts it to the front of the bathhouse to be installed. (The ritual master offers the formal announcement for the bath, saying:
"The bath chamber stands wide open, penetrating through all ten directions; the hot springs flow in full measure, circulating throughout the four seas."

I address you, O multitude of spirits: together you enter in great numbers, bathing as one in the profound waters of meditative stillness and perfuming yourselves thrice with the fragrant scent of the precepts.
Having completely forgotten the entanglements of karmic burdens, how could any delusions remain? No longer do forms and appearances alternate in perception;
there is only Suchness. This is not merely a matter of empty talk; it must be realized through the attainment of wondrous awakening.
I shall now reverently recite the *Bathing Mantra* of our Buddha, the Tathāgata.
Oṃ tiṣya tiṣya saṃgha svāhā. (Having completed three recitations of the mantra, the assembly of practitioners strikes gongs and cymbals and sings praises.

The ritual master proceeds to the bathhouse to perform the purification rite. The Dharma Master visualizes this bathhouse as vast, majestic, and pure, naturally radiant with light, where the countless sentient beings of the six realms [gather].)

The assembly, having heard the aforementioned Dharma-sounds, all entered therein to bathe. By the power of the Dharma, they did not obstruct one another; their bodies and minds were refreshed and joyful, attaining great peace and bliss. (The ritual master rings the bell and recites the verses of praise, saying:)
The six realms and four modes of birth are all the Dharma-realm; whether hidden or manifest, their numbers are immeasurable.
Their diverse names and various titles are but empty appellations; their wondrous features and inferior forms are all illusory substances.
Coming and going in an instant, they are like glances through a crevice; arising and ceasing in an instant, they are equal to floating bubbles.
All have lost their original luminosity in a single thought, Thereby causing them to take on bodies as retributions for delusion.
On this day, the donor initiates a universal salvation; The assembly of Buddhas and devas gathers in solemn purity.
I look up to rely upon your compassionate power for support, To gather in all living beings without exception.
To cause them to take refuge and return to the Right Path, one must first bathe them to cleanse all external dust;
once the external dust is purified and the inner mind is harmonized, they may then advance to receive the Dharma-offering.

(After the bath is finished. [The Ritual Master recites the *biaobai* (declaration), rings the bell, and offers clothing to the six realms of existence. Before the bathhouse, he burns paper garments for the deceased; if none are available, this step is omitted. He then makes the following declaration:]

Entering the chamber, one awakens to the cause of water; having clearly manifested wondrous touch, one bathes the body to remove dust and defilement, thereby maintaining solemnity in outward deportment.
Through personally receiving the empowerment of the Buddha’s power, one is enabled to entirely restore the original form of the human being.

Realizing that all are of one and the same mark, one unifies those myriad differences. As one draws near to the Honored Countenance, one must adorn oneself with magnificent robes. Thus it is proclaimed.
By means of the secret mantras and illuminating them with subtle and profound contemplation, one gives rise to pure conditions that support and perfect impartial giving.

Celestial robes naturally drape the body without waiting for intentional seeking; the Dharma-medicine is universally bestowed, permeating the mind—so what need is there to discuss being moved by recitation?

Because my own aspirations are rooted in the wish to benefit others, the practices cultivated by others will likewise be of benefit to me. By extending this principle through analogy, there is nothing that cannot be accomplished.
The Buddha, the Tathāgata, possesses a mantra for consecrating robes; I shall now reverently recite it.
Oṃ vīmukta-niyama-vaśeṣṭhi-cūru cūru svāhā. (Having recited this mantra three times, ring the ghaṇṭā and cymbals.

(The Dharma Master visualizes the countless multitudes of sentient beings in the six realms of existence; by the power of the Dharma, they all take human form, with upright and handsome features, their bodies naturally adorned with clothing.)
Their dignified deportment was majestic and imposing; they were filled with immeasurable joy. The ritual master, ringing the bell, summoned them in and addressed them:

"Without washing away the dust or cleansing the body, you have already attained wondrous realization through perfect penetration. You must surely shake out your robes and adjust your caps, and further cultivate your countenance and demeanor;
only then may you participate in this unobstructed assembly. This is the gateway to ascending to Great Enlightenment. Thus spoke the long-standing practitioner.
For those of deep capacity, their spiritual nature will shine forth brilliantly here; for those with heavy self-obstructions, their karmic habits will be suddenly forgotten upon reaching this point.
I pray to receive the Master’s instruction, so that this very night I may know where to return. This is most agreeable to my heart; I shall surely attain liberation in this very body.
"Fortunately, we have heard these excellent instructions; you should now proceed with joyful haste.

(The assembly strikes the cymbals and escorts the *jingdao* [purification path] to the center outside the ritual hall, where it is installed. Offerings of flowers and other items are arranged accordingly. Furthermore, a plaque is first set up outside the purification path, inscribed with the words:
"All sentient beings of the six realms and below, as well as the spirits for whom this memorial service is held, stand here in succession to pay homage to the Triple Gem.")
The Ritual Manual for the Auspicious Assembly of the Dharma Realm’s Holy and Mundane Beings on Land and Water, Scroll Three.
The Ritual Manual for the Auspicious Assembly of the Dharma Realm’s Holy and Mundane Beings on Land and Water, Scroll Four.
Carefully compiled by the Śramaṇa Zhìpàn of Donghú, Sìmíng, during the Song Dynasty.
Revised by the late scholar of Yung-ch'i in Ancient Hang-chou, Chu-hung. (A large black plaque is set up outside the ritual hall. Upon it, the following characters are inscribed:

"The various sentient beings of the six realms, including the deceased spirits for whom offerings are made, shall all stand here in order. Furthermore, small plaques are made, upon which are inscribed fourteen positions, including those of the lower hall and the accompanying seats.

Now, one such plaque is provided as a model: "The Four Emptinesses, the Four Dhyānas, the Six Desire Heavens, the Sun, Moon, and Star Heavens, and the Holy Multitudes of the Celestial Bureaucracy. The others follow this pattern; each consists of sixteen characters. These small plaques are arranged in front of the large plaque. Respectfully offered.

(To welcome the Pure Path, set it before the small tablet). (The Dharma Master, the assembly, and the patron stand to the side facing east). (The Ritual Director sets up a table and stands to the west; shaking the bell, he makes this announcement):
I address you, the six classes of ordinary beings: you are all gathered here as one assembly; who can distinguish between self and other? What interval can there be between kin and enemy?

It is by relying on the sustaining power of merit and the Dharma that one attains the equality of the spirit of giving and compassion. As you are about to approach this magnificent gathering, you must first practice the true ritual.
Regarding the so-called roots and objects that correspond to purity, one should proceed by means of the path of right conduct until one receives the precepts of non-action;
thus may one tread upon the Great Way. It is fitting that these be arranged in proper sequence, so that all may reverently listen to these exhortations.

(The Dharma Master visualizes the six realms of existence, as well as the deceased spirits and others, arrayed in successive order upon the Pure Path, like a sea of clouds. (The ritual master rings the bell and recites verses and mantras to purify the three karmas of the six realms.)
All you assembled spirits, gather together now; You shall personally take refuge in the Triple Gem.
Your physical forms are already fully adorned; Yet some may say that your speech and mind have not been purified.
Therefore, following the expedient path of the Tathāgata, We act to eliminate the multitude of transgressions of the three karmas.
Realizing true emptiness within this very thought, the six faculties are simultaneously stilled.
I now offer this for the sake of all sentient beings throughout the six realms of the Dharma-realm, universally causing their six sense organs and three karmas to be purified.
The Buddha has a mantra which I shall now reverently proclaim and recite:
Oṃ sarvabāva sarvadharma sarvabāva śodhaya. (Note:
*bā* and *ba* are both pronounced with the "wang" and "fu" initials; *śu* is pronounced with the "shu-lü" initials.)

(After reciting the mantra three times, ring the hand-bell and cymbals. (The Dharma Master visualizes that the three karmas and six sense faculties of all sentient beings in the six realms have each attained purity, free from defilement and obstruction.

The Dharma Master and the patron offer incense on behalf of the six realms. (The officiant strikes the bell and proclaims the verses, burning incense and paying homage for the sake of the six realms.)
O you multitudes of spirits who have wandered through beginningless kalpas, Drifting through the six realms without knowing where to turn—
How fortunate that tonight, by some karmic affinity, All within the Dharma-realm receive universal deliverance!
As we are now about to personally approach the assembly of the Triple Gem, We must first reverently burn a censer of incense.

Through these pure offerings, I manifest my sincere devotion; I pray that you will grant your compassion and accept them. Now, for the sake of all sentient beings throughout the six realms of the Dharma-realm, I offer this incense to communicate my message. There is a mantra of the Buddha: Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ sarvathā vidyā-rājñī svāhā. (Repeat three times) This incense is offered to the Buddhas of the ten directions and the Three Jewels. May it reach the presence of the Honored Ones and serve as a messenger to convey my sincerity. May the Honored Ones, out of their great compassion, graciously accept this offering. May all sentient beings of the six realms attain liberation from suffering and quickly realize the supreme, perfect enlightenment. May all obstacles be removed and all aspirations be fulfilled. May the Dharma-wheel turn everywhere, and may the teachings of the Buddha flourish and remain for a long time. May all beings dwell in peace and happiness. (Recite the Heart Sutra once) I now offer this incense to the Buddhas of the ten directions, the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, the Pratyekabuddhas, the Śrāvakas, and all the holy assembly of the Triple Gem. May they receive this offering with compassion and bestow their blessings upon me and all sentient beings. May we all quickly attain the fruit of Buddhahood. (Recite the Heart Sutra once) I now offer this incense to the various deities who protect the Dharma and the world, including the Four Heavenly Kings, the Eight Great Nāga Kings, the Twelve Zodiac Deities, the Twenty-Eight Lunar Mansions, the Five Planets, the Twelve Spirits, and all the spirits of the mountains, rivers, and forests. May they receive this offering with compassion and protect the Dharma and the nation, ensuring peace and stability. May all calamities be averted and all blessings increase. May all beings be free from fear and dwell in harmony. (Recite the Heart Sutra once) I now offer this incense to the spirits of the deceased, those who have passed away, and all wandering ghosts and spirits. May they receive this offering with compassion, find peace and liberation from suffering, and eventually attain rebirth in the Pure Land. May they never again fall into the evil realms. (Recite the Heart Sutra once) I now offer this incense to all the spirits of the earth, the spirits of the soil, the spirits of the fields, and all other spirits who inhabit this place. May they receive this offering with compassion and protect this dwelling, ensuring safety and prosperity. May all beings dwell in peace and happiness. (Recite the Heart Sutra once) I now offer this incense to all the spirits of the ancestors, both near and distant, and all those who have departed before. May they receive this offering with compassion, find peace and fulfillment, and be reborn in the higher realms. May they never again suffer in the lower paths. (Recite the Heart Sutra once) I now offer this incense to all the spirits of the household, the spirits of the kitchen, the spirits of the well, and all other spirits who reside within this home. May they receive this offering with compassion and protect the family, ensuring health and harmony. May all members of the household dwell in peace and joy. (Recite the Heart Sutra once) I now offer this incense to all the spirits of the surrounding environment, the spirits of the mountains, the spirits of the waters, the spirits of the winds, and the spirits of the clouds. May they receive this offering with compassion and protect all living beings, ensuring that the weather is favorable and the harvests are bountiful. May all beings dwell in peace and happiness. (Recite the Heart Sutra once) I now offer this incense to all the spirits of the night, the spirits of the dawn, the spirits of the day, and the spirits of the dusk. May they receive this offering with compassion and protect all living beings, ensuring that they are free from harm and anxiety. May all beings dwell in peace and happiness. (Recite the Heart Sutra once) I now offer this incense to all the spirits of the four seasons, the spirits of the five elements, the spirits of the eight winds, and the spirits of the twelve months. May they receive this offering with compassion and protect all living beings, ensuring that the cycles of nature are harmonious and that all things flourish. May all beings dwell in peace and happiness. (Recite the Heart Sutra once) I now offer this incense to all the spirits of the underworld, the spirits of the hells, the spirits of the hungry ghosts, and the spirits of the animal realm. May they receive this offering with compassion, find relief from their suffering, and eventually attain rebirth in the higher realms. May they never again suffer in the lower paths. (Recite the Heart Sutra once) I now offer this incense to all the spirits of the intermediate state, the spirits of transition, and all those who are wandering in uncertainty. May they receive this offering with compassion, find guidance and peace, and quickly attain rebirth in the Pure Land. May they never again be lost in the cycle of birth and death. (Recite the Heart Sutra once) I now offer this incense to all the spirits of the past, present, and future, and to all the spirits of the universe. May they receive this offering with compassion and protect all living beings, ensuring that the Dharma flourishes and the world is at peace. May all beings dwell in peace and happiness. (Recite the Heart Sutra once) I now offer this incense to all the spirits of the Dharma-protectors, the spirits of the Vinaya, and the spirits of the Sutras. May they receive this offering with compassion and protect the true Dharma, ensuring that it remains pure and uncorrupted. May the teachings of the Buddha spread far and wide. (Recite the Heart Sutra once) I now offer this incense to all the spirits of the Sangha, the spirits of the monasteries, and the spirits of the meditation halls. May they receive this offering with compassion and protect the community of practitioners, ensuring that they dwell in harmony and cultivate their minds with diligence. May all practitioners attain the Way. (Recite the Heart Sutra once) I now offer this incense to all the spirits of the lay followers, the spirits of the donors, and the spirits of those who have supported the Dharma. May they receive this offering with compassion and be reborn in the higher realms, where they may continue to support and propagate the true Dharma. May they never again fall into the lower realms. (Recite the Heart Sutra once) I now offer this incense to all the spirits of the local guardians, the spirits of the village, and the spirits of the neighborhood. May they receive this offering with compassion and protect this community, ensuring that all inhabitants live in safety and prosperity. May all beings dwell in peace and happiness. (Recite the Heart Sutra once) I now offer this incense to all the spirits of the deceased who have not yet found peace, those who have been forgotten, and those who are suffering in obscurity. May they receive this offering with compassion, find rest and liberation from their suffering, and eventually attain rebirth in the Pure Land. May they never again wander in the realms of suffering. (Recite the Heart Sutra once) I now offer this incense to all the spirits of the natural world, the spirits of the forests, the spirits of the oceans, and the spirits of the skies. May they receive this offering with compassion and protect all living beings, ensuring that the environment is harmonious and that all creatures thrive. May all beings dwell in peace and happiness. (Recite the Heart Sutra once) I now offer this incense to all the spirits of the Dharma-realm, the spirits of the ten directions, and the spirits of the three times. May they receive this offering with compassion and bestow their blessings upon me and all sentient beings. May we all quickly attain the supreme, perfect enlightenment. (Recite the Heart Sutra once) I now offer this incense to all the spirits of the Buddhas of the past, present, and future, and to all the Honored Ones of the Triple Gem. May they receive this offering with compassion and grant their protection and blessings. May all sentient beings be liberated from suffering and quickly realize the Way. (Recite the Heart Sutra once) I now offer this incense to all the spirits of the Dharma-protectors, the spirits of the Vinaya, and the spirits of the Sutras. May they receive this offering with compassion and protect the true Dharma, ensuring that it remains pure and uncorrupted. May the teachings of the Buddha spread far and wide. (Recite the Heart Sutra once) I now offer this incense to all the spirits of the Sangha, the spirits of the monasteries, and the spirits of the meditation halls. May they receive this offering with compassion and protect the community of practitioners, ensuring that they dwell in harmony and cultivate their minds with diligence. May all practitioners attain the Way. (Recite the Heart Sutra once) I now offer this incense to all the spirits of the lay followers, the spirits of the donors, and the spirits of those who have supported the Dharma. May they receive this offering with compassion and be reborn in the higher realms, where they may continue
I shall now reverently recite:
Oṃ śavali-ta ma-ni a-pra-ku-ṭha su-pa-ra-ni vi-kā-ḍhi huṃ.

(After reciting the mantra three times, strike the gong. (The Dharma Master visualizes clouds of incense pervading the ocean-like assembly before the Triple Gem and the holy sages, so that all sentient beings of the six realms may attain penetrating faith.
Without exception, he universally proclaims and rings the bell to recite the verses, thereby inviting the Triple Gem for the sake of the six realms.)
All you assembled spirits, now present in this assembly, Purify the three karmas so they are stainless and free from dust.
From now on, if you wish to enter the gateway of the Mahāyāna, You must first take refuge in the realm of the Triple Gem.
Those who have practiced in past lives should further cultivate their habits; Those newly beginning their studies in this life may take this as the cause.
To practice the supreme Dharma and take refuge, I now first earnestly entreat you with a sincere heart of devotion and prostration.

Throughout the entirety of empty space, pervading the entire Dharma-realm, to the Buddhas of the ten directions who dwell eternally (Chorus), together with all their retinues (The Dharma Master, the assembly, and the patrons, leading all sentient beings of the six realms, simultaneously perform prostrations; hereafter, all instances shall follow this pattern).

With a sincere heart, we take refuge and entreat you: throughout the entirety of empty space and pervading the Dharma-realm, to the eternally abiding Dharma-kāya of the ten directions (congregation joins), together with all your retinues.

With a sincere heart, we take refuge and entreat the Sangha of the ten directions, eternally abiding throughout the entirety of empty space and pervading the Dharma realm, together with all their retinues.
(The officiant addresses them: [Insert prayer here].
I now, on behalf of all sentient beings of the six realms within the dharma-realm, invoke the Triple Gem.
The Buddha has a mantra which I shall now recite: *Namo samanta-mudrāya oṃ uccā-pratīhata*.
*Tattva-sarvata-tāta kuśa-mati oṃ śrīya-mūla prākārya svāhā.* (Recite this mantra three times; strike the cymbals.

[The Dharma Master visualizes the clouds of the Triple Gem and the holy sages assembling at the seat to witness the ritual. The sentient beings of the six realms kneel with palms joined, requesting to receive the refuges and precepts. At that time, the Dharma Master prepares...]

[The Master] ascends the high seat and sits facing outward. (The *biaobai* [officiant] sits with the assembly on both sides; the patrons and others sit behind the assembly on both sides. (The Dharma Master sits cross-legged and preaches the Dharma for the sake of the six realms of existence to inspire faith.)

All sentient beings of the six realms within the Dharma-realm should know that the reason they are able to arrive at this Dharma assembly is due to the present patron’s ability to establish this Great Universal Salvation Retreat. Yet, to inquire about crossing the ford upon this Path—
One must give rise to faith. If the mind cannot yet believe, what is there in the Way? Regarding "faith," as the Dharma Master of Siming said:

"Believe that all phenomena are fundamentally possessed within the mind alone, and that they arise entirely from the mind. This refers to the two modes of creation—phenomenal and noumenal—as the objects of faith.
There is no separate principle for their arising; both proceed from what is fundamentally possessed. One believes that this phenomenal creation proceeds from [the fundamental].

This is the principle of inherent inclusion (*li-jù*). This inclusion has no separate existence; all things are produced through conditions. To believe in this inherent inclusion is precisely the manifestation of phenomena (*shi-zào*).

Thus, one knows that the characteristics of the world are eternal and that the principle of dependent origination is one. Having already understood that phenomena and principle are non-dual, one must further know that matter and mind are mutually interfused.
Therefore, every dharma is omnipresent and every moment is fully endowed with all things; the ten directions and the three periods of time are not...
Intermingled moments. All Buddhas and sentient beings are termed the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). This is the meaning of perfect faith in mutual possession and mutual creation.

Since one can believe that all phenomena are possessed by the mind and created by the mind, one must further know that, in reality, there is neither a creator nor that which is created, neither a possessor nor that which is possessed.
This is because the mind is itself the Dharma, and the Dharma is itself the mind. [The categories of] creator and created, possessor and possessed...

Whatever is possessed, in every instance, is nothing but this single mind; in every instance, it is nothing but this single form. Mind alone and form alone—when confronted with such duality, it vanishes.
When one contemplates them through wondrous observation, there is nothing that is not the Three Truths.
If this is so, then in every instance all is empty: when one is empty, all is empty. The entire body is provisional: when one is provisional, all is provisional. The two extremes cannot be grasped...
It is attained: within one, all are contained; within one mind, the three contemplations are present, their illumination neither vertical nor horizontal;
the three truths are a single realm, their essence neither concurrent nor distinct. Who does not possess this wondrous principle? The Buddhas of the three periods have already realized it;
all sentient beings are currently deluded regarding it. Though they are deluded throughout the day, they never depart from it. If one can truly believe this—

The principle of the Three Truths is such that the essence of the sages and ordinary beings is one. Thus, one may believe that this present assembly for the Dharma-giving takes the Three Jewels as its single embodiment as its place of refuge.
From the first generation of the bodhicitta until the ultimate attainment, everything is accomplished through the faith of this very day.
I pray that all sentient beings within the six realms will have deep faith in these words and take them forever as their reliance.
(The Dharma Master, from his seat, preached the Dharma for the six realms of existence. [He taught] taking refuge in the Three Jewels of the One Essence.
All sentient beings within the six realms of the Dharma-realm have already been able to fully give rise to the Great Mind and attain resolute faith.

Now, for your sake, I shall rely upon the holy teachings to provide a detailed explanation of the characteristics of the Three Jewels of the One Essence, so that you may know that they are equally possessed by both the sages and the ordinary. Next, I shall...
This correctly demonstrates the method of contemplating the Three Jewels within the mind, so that one may understand the mutual fusion of cultivation and nature.
Regarding the Three Jewels, as the Holy Master Tiantai said: "Before the Buddha appeared in the world, there was only the transformation of the Wheel-Turning King through the ten wholesome paths."
From the time the Great Sage first attained perfect enlightenment, he first bestowed the Three Refuges upon the elder Trapusa, causing him to turn away from heterodoxy and return to the truth;
this serves as the very foundation for entering the state of sainthood. These Three Refuges universally give rise to all categories of precepts as well as all supramundane wholesome dharmas;
therefore, they differ from the ancient method of the ten wholesome paths. As for what is called "taking refuge":
"Returning" (gui) has the meaning of turning back and returning. To turn away from false teachers and return to serve a true teacher—this is taking refuge in the Buddha.
To turn away from false teachings and return to cultivate the True Dharma—this is taking refuge in the Dharma.

To turn away from the ninety-five kinds of external paths and return to follow those who practice the correct path of the Three Vehicles—this is taking refuge in the Sangha. "Relying" (yi) has the meaning of depending upon.

Relying on the awakening of the mind, one attains transcendence from the three realms; this is relying upon the Buddha. Relying on the Dharma taught by the Buddha, one attains transcendence from the three realms; this is relying upon the Dharma.
Relying on the companions of the Three Vehicles, one attains transcendence from the three realms; this is relying upon the Sangha.
As for the term "Three Jewels," these—the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha—are worthy of honor and respect, and are therefore called "Jewels. Furthermore, there is the conventional [sense].

There is a principle and there are phenomena. Phenomena refer to the Three Jewels as they are maintained in the world. Principle refers to the Three Jewels as a single essence. Regarding "maintained":
when the Buddha was in the world, his attainment of the Way under the King of Trees was the Buddha Jewel; his preaching of the Dharma of the Four Truths was the Dharma Jewel;
and his ordination of the five bhikṣus was the Sangha Jewel. After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, images cast in metal or molded from clay, and paintings on paper or silk, constitute the Buddha Jewel.

The yellow scrolls and red registers—the holy teachings of the Tripiṭaka—constitute the Dharma Jewel. Those who shave their hair and dye their robes to propagate the Buddha’s transformation constitute the Sangha Jewel.
Because these three abide in the world without interruption, they are called the "Abiding Three Jewels. Furthermore, all images are the True Body;
wherever the scriptures reside is where the Buddha’s śarīra is found. Even ordinary monks of the present day are capable of shouldering the True Dharma.
They serve as the field of merit for the world; they are also the place of refuge. Regarding the "single essence":

through the wisdom of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), one awakens to all phenomena as being neither empty nor existent, yet both empty and existent—a simultaneous negation and illumination. This perfect awakening of the three types of knowledge is called the Buddha Jewel.
The principle of the dharma-nature that is awakened to, in which the three truths are fully present, is called the Dharma Jewel. Such awakening...
Wisdom, when in harmonious union with principle and phenomena, is called the Sangha Jewel.

Thus, based upon the Dharma of Teaching, I have exhaustively explained the characteristics of the Three Jewels as One Entity to develop sublime understanding for you all—the myriad spirits of the six realms.
Now, for your sake, relying upon the Dharma of Practice, I shall correctly demonstrate the method for contemplating the Three Jewels within the mind. Therefore, Tiantai and Siming...
The words of the two masters state: "Contemplate with clarity that a single thought-moment is simultaneously empty, provisionally existent, and the Middle; this is itself the Three Jewels.
Just as the present single thought-moment of you, the myriad spirits of the six realms, inherently possesses the three truths, yet remains unawakened while in delusion—this is the Dharma Jewel.
The wisdom capable of awakening to these three truths is the Buddha Jewel. The union of the truths and wisdom is the Sangha."
The Jewel. The principle of reality (*tattva*) is the nature; the other two are cultivation. You all inherently possess these three dharmas within your nature.

Although you are deluded and do not realize them, the principle is fundamentally true and correct, and is thus called the Dharma-Jewel. When cultivation arises fully from this nature, the wisdom of the three truths is perfected, whereby one is able to awaken;
this is called the Buddha-Jewel. When this wisdom and the nature are in mutual correspondence and harmonious union, it is called the Sangha-Jewel. To investigate this further in detail:
The three nines (twenty-seven) open and close; fearing prolixity, I shall not enumerate them all. Thus, by taking refuge in the Triple Gem, all dharmas of the Path arise spontaneously.
Even those at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) must still take refuge, let alone those from the stages of the *bhūmis* downward.

Even the noble ones of the Two Vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) must still take refuge, let alone the ordinary beings of the six realms. I now do this specifically for you all. I offer [this teaching].

Practice this taking of refuge, so that those who possess roots of goodness from past lives may thereby reach maturity, and those who have not yet resolved to attain enlightenment may plant their seeds herein.
You should know that you yourselves inherently possess the Three Jewels in their unified essence; this is the cause capable of evoking a response.

The Buddhas have already realized the Three Jewels in their unified essence; these are the conditions capable of responding. It is solely because the way of resonance and response is never errant [that this occurs].
Thus, the principle of transmission and reception is now established. I shall now lead the chant of taking refuge.
You multitudes of spirits from the six realms, purify your three karmas and kneel reverently before me; with single-minded diligence, seek [the Way] and listen to my words.

I, disciple [Name], from this present body until the attainment of Buddhahood, take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Sangha. (The assembled assembly, the host of the feast, and the spirits of the six realms, following the instructions of the Dharma Master, chant together three times.
The Dharma Master then addresses them:)
The conferral of the Three Refuges has now been completed. To further perfect the Dharma, three additional recitations are added:
"I, the disciple [Name], have taken refuge in the Buddha;
I have taken refuge in the Dharma; I have taken refuge in the Sangha" (recite as before).
From this day forward, we take the Buddha as our teacher. We pray only that the Triple Gem will look upon us with compassion and accept us. (Recite the preceding three times;

the assembly bows and pays homage to the Buddhas, Dharmas, Sanghas, and Dharma Masters of the ten directions who eternally abide, and declares for the sake of those traveling through the six realms of existence who practice the Mahāyāna Repentance Rite: (As before, recite three times; the assembly prostrates and pays homage to the Buddhas, Dharmas, Sanghas, and Dharma Masters of the ten directions who eternally abide, and makes this declaration for those practicing the Mahāyāna Repentance Rite of the Six Realms.)

"You all, the myriad spirits of the six realms, having already been able to take refuge in the Triple Gem and become disciples of the Buddha, should further seek the Bodhisattva Mahayana precepts as the eternal foundation for attaining Buddhahood.

However, because you have, from time immemorial, wandered through the various realms of existence and accumulated heavy karmic offenses, these have served as obstructions. Now, for your sake, based on the Great..."
The Gateway of the Vehicle: Practicing the Method of Repentance so that Body and Mind are Radiant and Pure, One is Then Fit to Receive the Precepts.
Regarding repentance, as the Holy Master of Tiantai stated, one must know the name of repentance, know the locus of repentance, and know the method of repentance.
Knowing the stage of repentance (*pratikramaṇa*). Regarding the name of repentance: the Sanskrit term is *kṣamā*, which here means "to repent of one's transgressions.

To sincerely take refuge in the Triple Gem and repent for one’s primary offenses constitutes knowing the name of repentance. Regarding the place of repentance, the *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-dhyāna-sūtra* states:
"If one wishes to repent, sit upright and contemplate the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). My own mind is inherently empty; neither sin nor merit has a master. Relying on...

This contemplation of the mind, which knows the true nature of transgressions, is the locus of repentance. Regarding the method of repentance, there is both the phenomenal (the event) and the noumenal (the principle).

The noumenal is correct contemplation; the phenomenal is the auxiliary path. Correct contemplation is precisely the contemplation of the dharma-nature. Dharma-nature is the true reality of all dharmas.

The auxiliary path consists of bodily circumambulation and prostration, verbal recitation, and mental exhortation and contemplation. These are practiced through the union of the primary and the auxiliary.
This is the method of repentance (*pratideśanā*). Regarding the stage of repentance, its significance is most extensive.

You, the various spirits of the six realms, if you commit the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*), the ten evil deeds (*daśākuśala*), or various other unwholesome precepts, and if you harbor evil thoughts moment by moment and associate with evil companions, this constitutes the causal karma for the hells.
You shall receive retribution in the hellish realm, undergoing extreme suffering from which you will not be liberated for vast eons. If there are those who... [text truncated]

To be attached to the five desires, to acquire wealth through unrighteous means, to benefit oneself by wronging others, and to be dull-witted and ignorant—these constitute the karmic causes for the realm of animals.
One shall receive retribution in the animal realm, where beings constantly harm one another with no way to put an end to it.

Furthermore, those who are stingy and greedy and do not practice giving, who hold false views and are deceitful, who break their fasts and violate the precepts, and who do not believe in cause and effect—these constitute the karma of hungry ghosts.
As for the cause: one shall receive the retribution of the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*), constantly suffering from hunger and thirst with no means of ever being satiated.

If there are those who cultivate meritorious deeds only sparingly, yet always harbor thoughts of surpassing others, who are arrogant and treat others with contempt, and who take great pleasure in litigation and dispute—this constitutes the karmic cause of the asuras.
One shall receive the retribution of the asura realm, where instruments of suffering arrive three times each day. Such individuals must perform repentance to extinguish [these karmas].

To eliminate karmic obstructions: if one has been negligent in upholding the fundamental social norms and the five precepts, these constitute the causes for human existence, and one should receive retribution in the human realm.
Yet, within the human realm there are eight sufferings, and one further commits various kinds of unwholesome acts, leading to a fall into the evil paths after death.
Such offenses must be repented so that karmic obstructions may be extinguished. As for practicing the ten paths of wholesome action, one should cultivate...

Worldly meditative concentration is the cause for the karma of the heavens; one shall receive the retribution of rebirth in the celestial realms. Yet, within the heavens there are the five signs of decay;
becoming addicted to sensual pleasures and failing to practice, one’s merit is exhausted and one falls back down. There are even those who descend directly from the upper realms into hell.

One must therefore perform repentance to extinguish and eliminate karmic obstructions. Beyond this, there is further wandering through the six realms of existence, undergoing the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
Regarding the body’s migration according to karma: there are those who encounter adverse conditions and do not complete their natural lifespan, resulting in an untimely death;
or there are violent spirits who watch for a person's vulnerability, seeking to bring about calamity or to consume them, or even inflicting further harm.
For all such cases, one should collectively perform repentance to eliminate karmic obstructions. This is what is meant by "recognizing the stage of repentance."
The above has been discussed by way of the six mundane realms. Now, regarding those who should perform repentance within the stages of the sages:

although the sages of the three vehicles in the two teachings of the *Āgama* (Tripitaka) and *Vaipulya* (Shared) differ in their methods of analyzing form or realizing the essence of form to enter emptiness, and differ in their skillfulness or clumsiness regarding what lies within and beyond the realms, they are alike in that they eliminate the four abidings (*catur-vāsa*) and equally realize partial emptiness (*pratyekāśūnyatā*).
Yet, while they have departed from the extremes of annihilation and permanence, they have not yet heard of Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).

Therefore, one must perform repentance to eliminate karmic obstructions. Although those of the Separate Teaching (Biaojiao) may reach the stage of the Ten Abodes (Shixiang), they still practice the Middle Way but have not yet realized it;
although they pass through the Ten Grounds (Shidi), they still realize the Middle Way but have not yet escaped subsequent obstructions;

even up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (Dengjue), they have not yet attained the state of No-more-learning (Wuxue). For this reason, one must perform repentance to eliminate karmic obstructions. This is just as in the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) at the [Ten] Abodes...

Abiding [in the stages] up to Equal Enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi), the wisdom and the severance of afflictions of the Dharma-body are not yet fully perfected; this is likened to the moon on the fourteenth night.

For this reason, one must also perform repentance to eliminate karmic obstructions. From the karma of the Avīci hell up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment in the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao), every position possesses three types of obstacles:
the number of afflictions, the categories of bound karma, and the variations in retributive suffering, all of which encompass and intermingle with the ordinary state.
Therefore, the *Sūtra on the Fiftyfold Calculation* states: "Up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment, all must perform repentance. This is precisely that meaning.
Now, although the two deaths have already perished and the three delusions are eternally severed—belonging to the Buddha alone—all other sages and worthies still require repentance;
how much more so for those in the six realms? I now, on behalf of all sentient beings within the six realms, perform this repentance according to the Mahāyāna sūtras.
The Method for Repentance: Before the Triple Gem, one should confess and repent openly. Those who practice repentance will attain purity of body and mind;
in every thought-moment, they shall behold Samantabhadra Bodhisattva and the Buddhas of the ten directions.
You should each, with a sincere heart, follow what I say: "I, [Name], with a sincere heart, repent."
The ocean of all karmic obstructions arises entirely from deluded thoughts.
If you wish to repent, sit upright and contemplate the true nature of reality. All transgressions are like frost and dew; the sun of wisdom can eliminate them.
Therefore, with a sincere heart, you should repent for the six sense faculties.

(The Dharma Master chants three times. The assembly responds in unison. The Dharma Master leads the beings of the six realms in a threefold harmony, exhorting the multitudes of spirits in the six realms to resolve upon Bodhicitta. "O you multitudes of spirits in the six realms:

from the beginningless past until the present, throughout the intervening time, there have surely been many among you who, during the eras of former Buddhas, encountered spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) who instructed you to resolve upon the mind [of awakening] and seek the path of Bodhi. Yet, it is only because of the afflictions (*kleśa*) of your past lives..."
Our obstructions are thick, the power of our vows and practices is feeble, and our resolve is not firm. Should we encounter even slight adverse conditions, we immediately fall back and lose our way;
or we may be born in places where the Buddha-dharma has not been heard, following various worldly and evil dharmas—how could we possibly give rise to the bodhicitta?
Now, by what good fortune have we encountered this donor’s establishment of a supreme assembly for a great vegetarian feast of universal salvation? Having already relied upon...
Regarding the Mahāyāna practice of repentance, one should immediately give rise to the great mind of bodhicitta with fierce resolve.
How, then, should this bodhicitta be generated? What is called "bodhi"? As the Venerable Master Tiantai said:

"The Buddha’s bodhicitta arises from great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*); among the Buddha’s correct practices, this mind is the foremost. Those who wish to seek the Buddha-way must first, by means of..."
Compassion perfumes the mind; even after attaining the fruit [of enlightenment], those who wish to transform others must likewise take this great compassion as their foundation.
Regarding the term *bodhi*: as stated in the *Miaofa lianhua jing xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra), the Sanskrit word *bodhi* is translated here as "Way" (*dao*).
There are three kinds of *bodhi*: first, *tathatā-bodhi* (the *bodhi* of true nature), which takes principle as the Way. Second, [the *bodhi* of practice]...
First is the Bodhi of Real Wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*); this takes wisdom as its path. Second is the Bodhi of Expedient Means (*upāya*);

this takes adapting to circumstances to accord with principle as its path. Thereupon, one contemplates the inconceivable realm (*acintya-viṣaya*). Based on the Four Noble Truths of Non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*), one establishes the Four Great Vows and gives rise to the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā-citta*).
Relying on the Truth of Suffering, one vows to deliver boundless sentient beings; relying on the Truth of Origination...
"I vow to sever the inexhaustible afflictions. These two vows are for the purpose of transforming sentient beings below. "I give rise to a heart of great compassion;
relying on the Truth of the Path, I vow to study immeasurable Dharma-gates; relying on the Truth of Cessation, I vow to achieve the unsurpassed Buddha-way.

These two vows are for the purpose of seeking the fruit of Buddhahood above. Now, on behalf of the multitudes of spirits in the six realms, I shall, in reliance upon this wondrous meaning, generate [this resolve].
Regarding the Four Great Vows, each should with a sincere heart follow what I say:
I, [Name], with a sincere heart, make this vow:
"Sentient beings are boundless; I vow to deliver them all. Afflictions are inexhaustible; I vow to sever them all."
I vow to study the immeasurable Dharma gates; I vow to realize the unsurpassed Buddha-way.
(The Dharma Master chants three times; the assembly responds in unison, uniting the six realms in harmony. (The Dharma Master preaches the precepts for the sake of the six realms.)
"You multitudes of spirits within the six realms, having already been able to repent and make vows by means of the Mahāyāna gate,

you should now with a sincere heart further seek the Dharma of the precepts. Indeed, the wondrous precepts of the three clusters of non-action (*asaṃskṛta*) of the Mahāyāna are the great raft for crossing the ocean of birth and death,
the skilled physician for curing the grave illness of heavy evil, the essential gateway for realizing the path to Nirvāṇa, and the [means] for entering the rank of all Buddhas."

This is the correct path. When the Buddhas appear in the world, their resolve is to propagate the transformative teachings. The methods for such transformation are said to be precept (śīla), concentration (samādhi), and wisdom (prajñā).
However, that which is cultivated by one of perfect capacity results in the perfection of all at once. Therefore, training in the precepts is itself training in concentration and wisdom;

training within a single mind ensures that there is nothing that is not universally encompassed. As for the term "precept" (śīla), it carries the meaning of prohibition. Regarding the characteristics of the precepts, in the Mahāyāna...
The three clusters of precepts (*trisaṃvara*) are named in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*. That which is called "restraint of conduct" (*saṃvara-śīla*) means that there is no evil that is not severed.

That which is called "gathering wholesome dharmas" (*kuśaladharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*) means that there is no wholesome dharma that is not cultivated. That which is called "benefiting sentient beings" (*sattvārtha-kriyā-śīla*) means that there is no sentient being who is not delivered.
Now, for your sakes, I shall further provide a detailed exposition of the essence of the precepts (*śīlaskandha*) as they are received. Thus, the Holy Master Tiantai—
It is said: Regarding the essence of the precepts (*śīla-tattva*), it is simply non-arising. If it arises, it is unconditioned derivative form (*avijñapti-rūpa*) which is its nature.

This means that if this essence of the precepts does not arise, it remains as such; if it does arise, it is entirely of the nature [of the precepts]. Thus, nature and cultivation are mutually perfected. The mind possesses unconditioned derivative form.
As for "derivative form," it is because the nature must rely upon derivative form-dharmas to manifest itself. Once the unconditioned [form] is once produced, one spontaneously ceases from evil.
It functions spontaneously and performs wholesome deeds; it does not require repeated effort, and is therefore called "unconditioned" (*anabhisaṃskāra*).

Unless one regresses from the bodhicitta, studies heterodox teachings, gives rise to superior evil intentions, or commits the ten grave offenses, then even if one falls into the three evil realms in future lives, one will ultimately never lose this precept.
If one later receives the Bodhisattva precepts again, it is not called "newly acquired," but is termed "revelation."
"Polished and pure. This means that one has once again been shown the meaning of what was already heard, and has polished the essence of what was already attained.
How sublime! Such is the excellence of the Dharma of the precepts. Now, for the sake of you all in the six realms, I shall perform the *karmavācanā* (ritual procedure).
You should each listen with a sincere mind to the performance of the rite. All sentient beings of the ten dharma-realms and the six realms—[the rest of the text follows]...
Spirits!

All you sons of the Buddha, listen attentively. You now seek from me to receive all the training precepts of the bodhisattvas, all the pure ethical discipline of the bodhisattvas—namely, the ethical discipline of restraint, the ethical discipline of gathering virtuous dharmas, and the ethical discipline of benefiting sentient beings.
These training rules, these pure precepts: all bodhisattvas of the past have already received them, studied them, understood them, practiced them, and perfected them;
all bodhisattvas of the future shall receive them, study them, understand them, practice them, and perfect them.
All bodhisattvas of the present now receive, now study, now understand, now practice, and now accomplish [this], and shall become Buddhas in the future.
From this body until the Buddha-body, you must not commit any transgression during the interval between them. Are you able to uphold this?

(The Dharma Master recites this three times. The great assembly, representing the convergence of the six realms and the three harmonies, is able to uphold it. The Dharma Master contemplates the multitudes of spirits across the six realms, each diligently applying the three karmas and receiving the pure precepts. Thereupon, a kind of wholesome dharma is induced to flow into their bodies and minds;
this constitutes the form of the unmanifest wholesome karma that has been generated. This form is subtle and exquisite, visible only to the divine eye).
This first round of the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) is completed. By the power of the mental karma of this sublime and virtuous precept-dharma, the worlds of the ten directions all tremble.
Listen attentively, O sons of the Buddha! You shall now receive from me all the training rules (*śikṣāpada*) for bodhisattvas (and so forth).
(As before, up to: "Are you able to uphold it?
This is the second *karmavācanā* completed. The wondrous and virtuous precepts of the ten directions now appear in the void like clouds or a canopy, covering the crown of your head.
"O sons of the Buddha, listen attentively! You now receive from me all the training precepts for bodhisattvas (as before, up to: Are you able to uphold them?"

This is the third *karmavācanā*, which has been completed. The wondrous and virtuous precepts of the worlds of the ten directions shall flow from the crown of your head into your body and mind, filling your primary retribution and forever becoming the seed of Buddhahood.
Thus far, I have thrice proclaimed the *karmavācanā* for you, the assembly of Buddha-sons from the six realms, and transmitted the precepts.
Since the ritual has been completed, this constitutes the attainment of the precepts.
(The Dharma Master expounds the ten grave precepts for the sake of the six realms of existence, as the method for maintaining and guarding them with a devoted mind.

You, the assembly of Buddha-sons from the six realms, having relied upon the Triple Gem and generated the unconditioned precepts (*anabhisaṃskāra-śīla*), have personally heard the *karmavācanā* and thereby established wholesome karma.
You ought from this point forward to maintain and guard them firmly; do not allow them to be violated in any circumstance.
Even if one commits an offense, it shall not cause distress or cause the mind to regress; even if distracted by sensory objects, the will shall not be deluded.

It is better to die with the precepts than to live without them. Even if one’s practice of the vehicle is urgent while the observance of the precepts is lax, one may encounter Maitreya with a body from the three miserable realms, hear the Dharma, and transcend the world.

How does this compare to maintaining pure precepts, realizing the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), and [attaining liberation] with a human or celestial body? How much more so when compared to [the state of] a nāga?

In the first assembly of the Flower Adornment Sutra, how could one have attained the highest grade of rebirth in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang) with this very body—possessing all precepts and practices and fully developing the three minds—were it not for the power of receiving and upholding the precepts on this very day?
Thus, the cycle of saṃsāra is forever ended and the holy fruits may be ascended;
none of this is not due to the strength of the precept-observance received on this day. Now, I shall proclaim for you the Brahmajāla Sūtra.

Chapter on the Mind-Ground. The Ten Grave *Pārājika* Offenses are set forth to clarify the characteristics of upholding and violating [the precepts]. You must study them well and reverently uphold them.
First is the Precept against Killing. The Buddha said: "O Son of the Buddha, if one kills by oneself, instructs others to kill, employs means to kill, or praises killing..."

Seeing this, one should rejoice. Even regarding incantations for killing—the cause of killing, the conditions for killing, the methods of killing, and the karma of killing—one must not intentionally kill any living being whatsoever.
This Bodhisattva should give rise to a mind of constant compassion and a mind of filial piety.
To use skillful means to rescue and protect all sentient beings, yet instead act with a self-indulgent and pleasure-seeking mind to kill living beings—this is a *pārājika* offense for a bodhisattva.

Second is the precept against stealing: O sons of the Buddha, whether one steals oneself, teaches others to steal, uses skillful means to steal, steals by incantation, or through the causes and conditions of stealing... stealing.

Conditioned by the taking of things that belong to others—whether they be the property of spirits or ghosts, or stolen goods belonging to thieves, or any other wealth down to a single needle or blade of grass—one must not intentionally steal them.
Rather, a Bodhisattva should give rise to a mind of filiality toward the Buddha-nature, a mind of compassion, and should constantly assist all people in generating merit and happiness.
If, on the contrary, one steals the property of others, this constitutes a transgression for a Bodhisattva.
The Pārājika offense.

The third precept against sexual misconduct: If a disciple of the Buddha indulges in sexual conduct himself, teaches others to engage in sexual conduct, or even intentionally commits sexual misconduct with any woman—due to the causes of lust, the conditions of lust, the methods of lust, or the karmic actions of lust—even with the females of animals, or the females of devas and ghosts.
Furthermore, if a Bodhisattva engages in sexual misconduct— failing to give rise to a mind of filial obedience and instead failing to protect all sentient beings and bestow the pure Dharma upon them—
and conversely gives rise to sexual desire toward all people, making no distinction between animals and even one's mother,
daughter, sister, or other six types of close relatives, and acts without a heart of compassion, this constitutes a *pārājika* offense for that Bodhisattva.

The fourth precept against false speech: If a disciple of the Buddha speaks falsely himself, teaches others to speak falsely, employs skillful means to speak falsely, or provides the causes, conditions, methods, and karmic actions for speaking falsely—even to the point of claiming to have seen what was not seen or claiming not to have seen what was seen—this constitutes physical and mental falsehood.
Yet, the Bodhisattva constantly gives rise to right speech and right view, and likewise inspires all sentient beings to do so.

To possess right speech and right view, yet conversely give rise to all manner of wrong speech, wrong views, and wrong actions among sentient beings—this constitutes a *pārājika* offense for a bodhisattva.

Fifth is the precept against selling alcohol: If a son of the Buddha sells alcohol himself, teaches others to sell alcohol, provides the means for selling alcohol, or encourages the selling of alcohol...
Regarding the conditions: the method of selling liquor, the business of selling liquor—no kind of liquor whatsoever may be sold.

Since such liquor is a causal condition for the arising of offenses, yet a Bodhisattva ought to give rise to the wisdom of clarity and penetration in all sentient beings, to instead further give rise to the minds of perversion in all sentient beings constitutes a *pārājika* offense for that Bodhisattva.

The sixth precept concerns speaking of the faults of the fourfold assembly. If a disciple of the Buddha, with their own mouth, speaks of the faults of renunciant or lay bodhisattvas, bhikṣus, or bhikṣuṇīs;
or teaches others to speak of their faults, the causes of their faults, the conditions of their faults, or the nature of their faults.

Regarding sinful karma: when a bodhisattva hears externalists, evil persons, or those of the two vehicles speak of what is neither Dharma nor Vinaya within the Buddha-dharma, they always give rise to a mind of loving-kindness and teach these evil people, causing them to develop wholesome faith in the Mahāyāna.
If a bodhisattva, on the contrary, speaks of the faults and transgressions within the Buddha-dharma themselves, this constitutes a *pārājika* offense for that bodhisattva.

Seventh is the precept against praising oneself and disparaging others: "O Sons of the Buddha, if one praises oneself and disparages others, or teaches others to praise themselves and disparage others—whether through the causes of disparaging others, the conditions of disparaging others, the methods of disparaging others, or the karma of disparaging others—a bodhisattva should instead act on behalf of all..."
If sentient beings receive honor while one receives insults; if misfortunes are directed toward oneself while good fortune is given to others;
and if one exalts one's own virtues, conceals the good deeds of others, and causes others to suffer humiliation—this constitutes a *pārājika* offense for a bodhisattva.

The eighth precept concerns stinginess and disparagement. If a Buddha’s disciple is stingy themselves, teaches others to be stingy, or engages in the causes of stinginess, the conditions for stinginess, the methods of stinginess, or the karmic actions of stinginess—then when that Bodhisattva sees any poor person coming to beg, they should provide according to what that person requires.
If a bodhisattva, with a malicious mind or a mind of anger, fails to give even a single coin, a single needle, or a single blade of grass;

or if there is one who seeks the Dharma, yet they do not explain to them even a single word, a single verse, or a portion of the Dharma as small as a mote of dust, and instead reviles and insults them—
this constitutes a *pārājika* offense for that bodhisattva.
The ninth is the precept against the angry mind refusing to accept repentance.

If a disciple of the Buddha becomes angry themselves, teaches others to be angry, or engages in the causes of anger, the conditions for anger, the methods of anger, or the karmic actions of anger, then that Bodhisattva ought to cultivate roots of goodness and non-contention toward all sentient beings, constantly giving rise to a heart of compassion and a heart of filial obedience.
Yet, instead, they act contrary to this toward all sentient beings, even toward those who are not...
Among sentient beings, if one reviles them with harsh speech, strikes them with the hand, or attacks them with knives or staves, and yet the mind does not cease;
even when the other person seeks reconciliation and offers apologies with kind words, if the anger is still not resolved, this constitutes a *pārājika* offense for a bodhisattva.

The tenth precept against slandering the Triple Gem: If a disciple of the Buddha personally slanders the Triple Gem, teaches others to slander the Triple Gem, or engages in the causes of slander, the conditions for slander, the methods of slander, or the karmic actions of slander;

and if that Bodhisattva, upon hearing even a single word of slander against the Buddha from a non-Buddhist or an evil person, feels as though three hundred spears are piercing his heart—let alone when he himself speaks such slander—yet fails to give rise to a mind of faith or a mind of filial obedience.
If, on the contrary, one further assists evil persons or those with wrong views who slander [the Dharma], this constitutes a *pārājika* offense for a bodhisattva.
Above, I have specifically revealed the characteristics of the ten grave precepts for you all; you should uphold them.
If you can apply your mind in this way, it will constitute the practice of the Bodhisattva path. When vows and conduct are fully perfected, one may ascend to the ranks of the sages. Therefore—
Exhortation: You must all be most reverent and careful. (The Dharma Master descends from his seat and removes the mat; the assembly and the donors all rise and stand to the left and right.

(The Dharma Master offers incense and returns to join the assembly in standing recitation of the Buddha's name. The Ritual Master [Table-biao] performs the invocation for the six realms of existence, the recitation of the Buddha’s name, and the request for empowerment, speaking as follows:)
All sentient beings of the six realms, having now received the pure precepts,

must pay homage to the Mahāyāna and the eternally abiding Triple Gem and all noble sages before they may proceed to join this assembly. I now invoke the sublime names of the Triple Gem on their behalf,
hoping that by receiving its majestic power, they may be granted protection and empowerment.
Homage to the Original Teacher Śākyamuni Buddha. Homage to Amitābha Buddha.
Homage to Maitreya Buddha.
Homage to the Mahāyāna Sūtra of the Lotus of the Wonderful Dharma. Homage to the Great Vaipulya Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra.
Namo to the Mahāyāna Suvarṇaprabhāsottama Sūtra.
Namo to Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva. Namo to Samantabhadra Bodhisattva. Namo to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
(Recite each of the above three times. The assembly, representing the six realms of existence, shall together recite the Buddha’s name with one voice.)

(Standing to the right of the altar, holding the incense burner and reciting verses in praise of the Triple Gem, bowing before each seat, and gesturing with the hand-incense burner to lead the way for the six realms:
Your countenance is most wondrous and marvelous, Your radiance illuminates the ten directions. I have previously made offerings to you;
Now I come once more to draw near. Holy Lord, King among Devas, With a voice like that of the kalaviṅka bird.
To those who compassionately pity all sentient beings, we now pay homage;
with utmost sincerity, we take refuge and prostrate to all Buddhas seen throughout the ten directions and the entire Dharma-realm. (Chorus) All Buddhas.
With a sincere heart, I take refuge and pay homage. Seeing [the Buddha] seated at the site of enlightenment throughout the Dharma-realm of the ten directions—(Chorus:

To all the Honored Dharmas, with a sincere heart, I take refuge and pay homage. Seeing [the Buddha] seated at the site of enlightenment throughout the Dharma-realm of the ten directions—(Chorus: To the Sangha of all Bodhisattvas.
With a sincere heart, I take refuge and pay homage to all the Pratyekabuddhas throughout the ten directions and the entire Dharma-realm who are seen sitting at the site of enlightenment.
With a sincere heart, I take refuge and pay homage to all the Śrāvakas throughout the ten directions and the entire Dharma-realm who are seen sitting at the site of enlightenment.

With a sincere heart, I take refuge and pay homage to those who are seen sitting at the site of enlightenment throughout the dharma-realm of the ten directions— the ancestral masters and monks— with a sincere heart,
I take refuge and pay homage to those who are seen sitting at the site of enlightenment throughout the dharma-realm of the ten directions— the immortals possessing the five supernatural powers.

With a sincere heart, I take refuge and pay homage to those seen sitting at the site of enlightenment throughout the dharma-realm of the ten directions—the various devas who protect the Dharma—with a sincere heart, I take refuge and pay homage to them.
With a sincere heart, I take refuge and pay homage to those seen sitting at the site of enlightenment throughout the dharma-realm of the ten directions—the various great divine kings.

With a sincere heart, take refuge and pay homage. Behold them seated at the site of enlightenment, together with the ten great assemblies of Bodhisattvas throughout the Dharma-realm of the ten directions.

(When performing each prostration, the Dharma Master should visualize that the sons of the Buddha from the six realms, each accompanied by immeasurable multitudes, simultaneously perform prostrations, welcoming the sons of the Buddha from the six realms into the interior of the site of enlightenment.)
(Recite the altar-ascending mantra while ringing the bell and making this declaration:
Having received the precepts and discipline, I am now a child of the Buddha; thus, from the substance of the six classes of ordinary beings, I have obtained reliance upon the light of the Triple Gem.
In one place, they offered their sincere devotion and simultaneously prostrated themselves; greatly rejoicing at this encounter, they fully satisfied their long-held aspirations.
As they were about to solemnly enter the *maṇḍala*, they sought once more to receive the power of the Dharma in secret.
The Tathāgata, our Buddha, possesses a mantra for ascending the altar.
I shall now reverently recite it: Oṃ (1) mi-pu-la-padma-mūka (2) para-sara (3) para-miśatu (4) kuru-lu (5) svāhā.

(When the recitation of the mantra has been completed three times, strike the gongs. The assembly welcomes [the deity] to the ritual arena. After the circumambulation and the performance of the path have been finished, the Ritual Master shakes the bell to offer the seat and speaks:)
To contain Mount Sumeru within a mustard seed, and to manifest the realm of the Treasure King upon the tip of a hair—this is an inconceivable matter.
What concern has it with a mind of grasping? Herein lies the manifestation of Cao’s realization; there is nothing that is not the realm of wondrous adornment.

Without negating the myriad phenomena, how could they exist outside the ten directions of space? As the great assembly has come well, we rely on these auspicious conditions to gather together, regardless of high or low station.
All was orderly. Far and near were left none out. They bowed low with stooped bodies and hurried forward; they took their seats according to rank and sat composedly.
With a single thought of silent stillness, a hundred anxieties dissolved away. "Please wait for a short while; we shall proceed to perform the ritual offerings."
The Tathāgata, our Buddha, possesses the mantra for the corresponding seat of meditation.
I shall now reverently recite it: Oṃ vimagha padma-sunade dhara dharaṇi maṇḍale svāhā.

(Recite the mantra three times. Then, strike the gong. (The Dharma Master visualizes the Buddha-sons of the six realms and their immeasurable retinues, who, personally receiving the power of the Dharma, each obtain their seats. (The Dharma Master leads the patrons and the great assembly to temporarily leave the ritual arena to take their medicinal meal;
meanwhile, he instructs one person of sincere and reverent character to remain and guard the site.)
The Ritual Manual for the Auspicious Assembly of the Dharma Realm’s Holy and Mundane Beings on Land and Water, Scroll Four;
The Ritual Manual for the Auspicious Assembly of the Dharma Realm’s Holy and Mundane Beings on Land and Water, Scroll Five.
Carefully compiled by the Śramaṇa Zhìpàn of Donghú, Sìmíng, during the Song Dynasty.
Revised by the later disciple Zuhong of Yunqi in Ancient Hangzhou.
(The Dharma Master enters the ritual hall and offers incense; the patron offers incense and performs prostrations. (The Ritual Announcer rings the bell and presents incense, reciting a verse.)
I erect this great precious incense burner to open the Dharma offering; its fragrant breeze is rich and dense with the scent of sandalwood.
Among all living beings, there is not one who does not perceive it with their mind. Through this, may they awaken to the meaning of the Middle Way.
Our Buddha, the Tathāgata, possesses a mantra for burning incense; I shall now reverently recite it.
Oṃ śvalitāmani aprakūṭa suparṇi vikacite hūṃ. (Having recited this mantra three times, ring the hand-bell.

(The Dharma Master visualizes that clouds of incense fill the ritual arena, so that the multitude of sentient beings in the six realms are perfumed by its fragrance, their hearing is opened, and they attain awakening. (The Ritual Official sprinkles water for purification, rings the bell, and recites the verse.)
The deep, clear, numinous spring fills the precious vessel; One knows that its flow originates from the source of one’s own mind.
Realizing the true mechanism right where one is, It is sprinkled everywhere upon this Dharma assembly, leaving nothing impure.
Our Buddha, the Tathāgata, possesses a mantra for sprinkling purification (*praṇīta*). I shall now reverently recite it.
Oṃ vaśira śameye hūṃ phaṭ siri mahi svāhā. (Recite this mantra three times. Then ring the hand-bell and cymbals.

(The ritual master recites the prose liturgy while sprinkling water over the seats and mats, ensuring it reaches everywhere. (The Dharma Master visualizes that wherever the water reaches—upon the tables and mats—it becomes radiant, pure, and majestic. (The ritual master proclaims:)
The intention is to state:

Why do those from the six realms of existence gather so numerous and assemble all at once? It is by relying upon the Buddha’s power that they have been permitted to join this sacred site (*bodhimaṇḍa*).

They shall all conform to the true regulations, so that they may all partake of the pure offerings. To accomplish this Dharma-gift and rely upon their faith, I venture to set forth these diligent efforts.
To manifest the arousal [of the aspiration].
(Having finished reading the intent, strike the cymbals; the ritual master shakes the bell and declares:
I take refuge in the Triple Gem of the ten directions; May you deign to bestow your divine power as a support for the unseen realm.
I now partake of this food while reciting the mantra, so that all beings throughout the six realms may universally receive this offering.
(The *biaobai* [offering prayer] for the universal distribution of food says:

Now, as for all dharmas, their essence consists of the three virtues (*triguṇa*). Within the environment and its inhabitants, and within form and mind, what is there that is not fully present? Therefore, the Great...

From the *zhou* (trichiliocosm) to the ocean of lands, down to a single mote of dust; throughout the past, present, and future, within a single kṣaṇa and a single thought—this essence of the three virtues is nowhere not pervasive.
What are these three virtues? They are the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), Prajñā, and Liberation (*vimukti*). These constitute the three.
Each possesses permanence, bliss, self, and purity; these constitute the virtues. The Dharma-body is not merely the Dharma-body alone;
it must necessarily possess prajñā and liberation. It is the same for prajñā and liberation, which likewise mutually possess one another.

In the single mind of the person of the Perfect Teaching, these three virtues are complete—neither vertical nor horizontal—and are therefore likened to a "perfect *ī*. Because they pervade all places, they are designated as the "Secret Treasury. How magnificent!
This is the general characteristic of that *dharmatā*.
